1 Assessment Overview and Instructions
This examination assesses your ability to reason
about data quality in realistic scenarios. You will
encounter incomplete, inconsistent, and
ambiguous records. For each question, identify
the quality dimension at stake, propose a
diagnostic step, and justify a remediation
decision. Answers are evaluated on clarity of
reasoning, appropriate use of evidence, and
recognition of trade-offs. The paper is designed
for a 12-week module with 24 sessions and 48
teaching hours; allocate your time accordingly.
Simulated observations must be distinguished
from causal claims.
1.1 Section A: Data Quality
Foundations
This section tests foundational concepts. You
must define key dimensions such as
completeness, consistency, timeliness, and
accuracy, and apply them to short cases.
Questions require you to distinguish between
intrinsic and contextual quality, and to explain
how measurement choices affect conclusions.
Use the provided scenario descriptions and the
sample of 240 records across 4 sites to support
your answers. Avoid asserting causation from
cross-sectional patterns; instead, frame
plausible mechanisms and note what additional
evidence would be needed.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 1.
Figure 1: Data quality dimensions and diagnostic focus
1.1.1 Diagnosing Missing Values in
a Clinic Registry
A clinic registry contains missing values for
patient age and visit date. Some missingness
appears related to site and to whether the visit
was urgent. (a) Classify the missingness
mechanism you suspect and justify your choice.
(b) Propose two diagnostic checks using the
available 240 records across 4 sites. (c)
Recommend a handling strategy and explain
how it might bias downstream estimates. (d)
State one limitation of your recommendation
and what additional data would strengthen the
analysis. Your answer should distinguish
observed patterns from causal explanations.
1.1.2 Resolving Conflicting
Records Across Source Systems
Two source systems report different values for
the same entity. System A is updated within 2
days, while System B undergoes review every 5
days. (a) Describe a reconciliation procedure
that accounts for update latency and review
cycles. (b) Specify which record you would treat
as authoritative and why. (c) Explain how you
would document the decision for audit
purposes. (d) Identify a risk of your approach
and a mitigation. Use the comparison matrix in
the table to structure your reasoning, and avoid

accurate without evidence.

1.2 Assessing Timeliness and
Fitness for Use
Table 1: Comparison of source system update and
review cycles
A dashboard reports operational metrics with a
refresh lag. Users complain that decisions are
based on stale information. (a) Define
timeliness in this context and distinguish it from
accuracy. (b) Propose a fitness-for-use
assessment that considers the decision cycle
and the cost of delay. (c) Recommend one
process change and one measurement change.
(d) Explain how you would evaluate whether the
change improved decision quality, noting that
observed improvements may not be causal.
Refer to the schedule table for the intended
review cadence.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 2.
2 Section B: Applied
Reasoning and
Evidence
This section requires longer, scenario-based
reasoning. You will analyze a multi-site data
collection effort, interpret summary indicators,
and propose quality controls. The simulated
annual indicators for 2022 through 2025 show
output rising from 78.37 to 119.07 and cost
rising from 50.94 to 77.40, with operating
surplus from 27.43 to 41.67. Use these only as
context; do not infer causality. Your answers
should demonstrate structured thinking, explicit
assumptions, and awareness of ethical and
operational constraints.

2.1 Section B: Scenario-Based
Questions
Read each scenario carefully. You are expected
to identify the data quality issue, propose an
investigation, and recommend an action with
justification. Where numeric indicators are
provided, treat them as simulated canonical
outputs and note their limitations. Credit is
given for distinguishing correlation from
causation, for specifying what evidence would
change your conclusion, and for acknowledging
trade-offs between timeliness, cost, and
completeness. Use the provided tables to
organize your responses where appropriate.
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE
2.1.1 Multi-Site Consistency Audit
Design
A program collects data from 4 sites over 12
weeks, with 240 records in total. Site-level
counts vary, and some sites report different
definitions for a key field. (a) Design an audit to
assess consistency across sites. (b) Specify two
quantitative checks and one qualitative check.
(c) Propose a governance mechanism to resolve
definitional conflicts. (d) Explain how you would
report findings without overstating
generalizability. Note that differences across
sites may reflect operational context rather
than data quality failures.
2.1.2 Interpreting Simulated
Indicators with Caution
The simulated indicators show output growth of
51.9 percent from 2022 to 2025, alongside
changes in cost and operating surplus. (a)
Identify two alternative explanations for the
observed pattern. (b) Specify what additional
data would help distinguish among them. (c)
Discuss one risk of using these indicators for
performance evaluation. (d) Recommend a
reporting practice that communicates
uncertainty. Your answer must clearly separate
observed simulated values from causal claims
and note that the indicators are not validated
measures of quality.
2.2 Submission Requirements
and Marking Criteria
Submit your answers as a single document.
Clearly label each question and sub-part. The
total marks are distributed across reasoning
quality, use of evidence, recognition of
limitations, and clarity of expression. Answers
that assert causality without justification will
lose marks. You may use the tables to structure
comparisons, but tables do not replace written
justification. Late submissions are handled
according to program policy. Ensure that all
numeric claims are clearly attributed to the
provided simulated indicators and that
speculative statements are labeled as such.
When reviewing answers, check whether the
candidate explicitly states assumptions about
missing data mechanisms and whether those
assumptions are testable with the available
records.
Candidates should note that the simulated
indicators are presented for context only and
are not designed to support causal inference
about program performance.
A strong response will distinguish between data
quality problems that are intrinsic to the record
and those that arise from how the data are used
in a specific decision context.
Consider whether the candidate proposes a
feasible diagnostic step, such as comparing
distributions across sites or reviewing data
entry logs, rather than only recommending
deletion or imputation.
The reconciliation procedure should account for
update latency and review cycles, and the
candidate should explain how conflicts are
documented and escalated.
Look for acknowledgment that timeliness is
relative to the decision cycle and that a refresh
lag may be acceptable for some uses but not
others.
Candidates should identify at least one
limitation of their proposed audit, such as small
site-level counts or inconsistent definitions that
cannot be resolved with existing data.
When interpreting simulated indicators, credit
answers that propose alternative explanations
and specify what evidence would help
discriminate among them.
A good answer will avoid claiming that observed
improvements are due to a specific intervention

without a comparison group or before-after
design with controls.
Table 2: Simulated annual indicators for contextual
reference
The governance mechanism for definitional
conflicts should include a clear owner, a
decision log, and a process for communicating
changes to data users.
Candidates should recognize that missingness
related to site and urgency may induce bias if
handled by complete-case analysis, and they
should discuss the direction of potential bias.
For the timeliness question, look for a
distinction between data freshness and data
accuracy, and a recommendation that
addresses both process and measurement.
The audit design should include both
quantitative checks, such as consistency rates,
and qualitative checks, such as interviews with
site staff about definitions.
Answers should note that the simulated
indicators cover 2022 to 2025 and that trends
over this period may be influenced by changes
in scope or definitions.
Credit candidates who propose documenting
reconciliation decisions in an audit trail that
records the rationale, the date, and the
responsible person.
A strong response will explain how the
recommended handling strategy could bias
downstream estimates and what sensitivity
analysis could be used to assess robustness.
Candidates should avoid treating the simulated
output and cost figures as validated measures
of data quality; they are contextual indicators
only.
Look for explicit statements about what
additional data would strengthen the analysis,
such as data entry timestamps or site-level
process documentation.
The response to the multi-site consistency
question should consider whether definitional
differences are legitimate adaptations or
unintended inconsistencies.
Candidates should propose a reporting practice
that communicates uncertainty, such as ranges
or qualitative confidence statements, rather
than presenting point estimates as precise.
When evaluating process changes for
timeliness, credit answers that describe how
decision quality would be measured and how
confounders would be addressed.
A good answer will recognize that the 2-day
update and 5-day review cycles create different
windows of vulnerability for stale data.
Candidates should specify how they would
sample records for the audit and justify the
sample size relative to the total of 240 records.
Look for acknowledgment that the 4 sites may
have different operational contexts, which
affects the interpretation of cross-site
comparisons.
The marking criteria reward clarity and
structure, so candidates should use headings
and tables where appropriate but ensure that
written justification is complete.
Candidates should note that the 12-week
module and 48 teaching hours provide limited
time, so prioritization of diagnostic steps is
important.

A strong response will identify ethical
considerations, such as privacy and fairness,
when recommending data handling or
reconciliation strategies.

Credit answers that propose a feedback loop
where data quality findings inform updates to
definitions, collection processes, and training.
Candidates should explain how they would
validate the reconciled records against an
independent source or a gold-standard subset.
Look for recognition that the simulated
operating surplus figures depend on both output
and cost, and that changes in either can drive
the pattern.
When discussing fitness for use, candidates
should connect the assessment to specific
decisions and the consequences of acting on
stale or incomplete data.
A good answer will state what would count as
evidence against the proposed explanation and
how that evidence could be collected within
existing constraints.
Candidates should describe how they would test
for non-random missingness by comparing the
distribution of observed urgency levels across
sites with and without missing records.
A strong answer will note that the 240 records
may not be representative of all records if
sampling was not random, and will propose a
sensitivity check.
Look for a recommendation to stratify the audit
by site, given that the 4 sites may differ in data
entry practices and patient mix.
Candidates should explain how they would use
the 2-day update window to flag records that
are likely to be stale at the time of a decision.
Credit answers that propose a pilot
reconciliation on a small subset before scaling
up, to identify definitional conflicts early.
A good response will discuss how the 5-day
review cycle interacts with the update lag to
create periods when data are both stale and
unverified.
Candidates should specify how they would
document the rationale for any data exclusions,
including who approved the exclusion and
when.
Look for acknowledgment that the simulated
output growth of 51.9 percent may reflect
changes in data collection rather than true
performance.
A strong answer will propose comparing the
reconciled totals with an independent source,
such as administrative records or external
benchmarks.
Candidates should note that the 12-month
agreement period may limit the ability to
observe long-term trends or seasonal effects.
Credit answers that describe how they would
use the 24 sessions and 48 teaching hours to
prioritize which data quality dimensions to
address first.
A good response will recognize that the
operating surplus figures for 2022 to 2025
depend on both output and cost, and will
caution against interpreting them as quality
measures.
Candidates should explain how they would
handle conflicting definitions across sites, such
